title: Minimum Window Substring
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every substring versus a variable size sliding window with incremental counts.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two strings s and t, return the smallest substring of s that contains every character of t, including matching how many times each character repeats in t. Return an empty string if no such window exists.

blocks.text: Given two strings s and t, return the smallest substring of s that contains every character of t, including matching how many times each character repeats in t. Return an empty string if no such window exists.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Shortest Shopping Trip That Buys Everything on a List
blocks.text: Like walking down one long aisle of a store and finding the shortest continuous stretch of that aisle that contains every single item on a shopping list, including duplicates, without needing to backtrack.

blocks.caption: Find the smallest stretch of s that contains every character t requires

blocks.text: t needs two occurrences of "a", but s only has one available anywhere, so no valid window can ever exist, giving an empty string.
It helps to ask what changes between one window and the next one right beside it, rather than treating every substring as an independent problem.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Find All Anagrams in a String already showed that a sliding window's letter counts can be maintained incrementally instead of rebuilt from scratch, but that problem used a fixed window size, checked at every position.

Observation 2: Here, the window size itself is exactly what needs to be minimized, so a fixed size window will not do; instead, both a right pointer that grows the window and a left pointer that shrinks it need to move independently.

Observation 3: The natural strategy follows directly: expand the right pointer, incrementally updating counts, until the window happens to satisfy every requirement from t; then, while it remains valid, greedily shrink from the left as far as possible, recording the smallest valid window seen, since a smaller valid window is always at least as good as a larger one.

Observation 4: The moment shrinking breaks a requirement, expansion resumes, confirmed by tracing s equal to "ADOBECODEBANC" against t equal to "ABC" through several expand and shrink cycles, discovering progressively smaller valid windows, "ADOBEC", then "EBANC", then finally "BANC", the true minimum.

Recognizing that a valid window should always be shrunk as far as possible before resuming expansion is what turns this into a single pass with two independently moving pointers, instead of checking every substring separately.
Check every possible substring of s directly, and for each one, count its characters and verify whether it contains everything t requires, keeping track of the smallest valid one found.

items: For every starting index i and every ending index j at or after i, extract the substring.
Count its characters and check whether it satisfies every character requirement from t.
Keep the smallest substring that satisfies the requirement.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every possible substring is extracted and counted completely independently, so no substring's validity is ever missed.
A candidate only replaces the current best when it is both valid and strictly shorter, guaranteeing the final answer is the true minimum.
Checking every character in need against the window's counts directly matches the problem's exact requirement, including repeated characters in t.

blocks.text: Every possible substring is directly checked against every requirement from t, so the true smallest valid window is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed) in the worst case, recounting up to n characters for each of O(n squared) substrings.
Space: O(m), for the character count maps.

Limitation: consecutive windows overlap heavily, yet their character counts are rebuilt completely from scratch every single time, instead of being adjusted incrementally as the window grows or shrinks.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it recomputes a window's full character counts from scratch for every single one of the O(n squared) candidate substrings, even though neighboring windows share almost all of their characters.

What incremental counting fixes: adding one character when the window grows and removing one character when it shrinks keeps the counts correct with constant work per step, exactly as Find All Anagrams in a String already showed for a fixed size window.

What is different here: the window size is not fixed, it needs to be minimized, so growth and shrinkage must be driven independently, expanding to find validity and shrinking to minimize it.

The core idea: expand the right pointer until the window is valid, then greedily shrink the left pointer while it stays valid, tracking overall validity with a single "missing requirements" counter instead of comparing full count maps.

Use two pointers to maintain a sliding window, along with a running count of characters currently inside it and a counter for how many of t's distinct character requirements are currently satisfied. Expand the window by moving the right pointer forward until every requirement is satisfied, then shrink it by moving the left pointer forward as long as it remains valid, recording the smallest valid window seen along the way. Once shrinking breaks validity, expand the right pointer again and repeat.
A sliding window that expands to satisfy every requirement, then contracts to the smallest valid size before expanding again.

blocks.caption: Optimized: expand the window until valid, then shrink it as far as possible while staying valid

codes.python:
from collections import Counter


def min_window(s, t):
    need = Counter(t)
    missing = len(need)                                     # how many distinct characters are not yet satisfied
    window_count = {}
    left = 0
    best_left, best_right = 0, -1
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        window_count[ch] = window_count.get(ch, 0) + 1
        if ch in need and window_count[ch] == need[ch]:
            missing -= 1                                          # this character's requirement just got satisfied
        while missing == 0:                                     # window is currently valid, try to shrink it
            if best_right == -1 or right - left < best_right - best_left:
                best_left, best_right = left, right
            left_ch = s[left]
            window_count[left_ch] -= 1
            if left_ch in need and window_count[left_ch] < need[left_ch]:
                missing += 1                                          # shrinking broke a requirement
            left += 1
    return s[best_left:best_right + 1] if best_right != -1 else ""


if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = "ADOBECODEBANC"
    t = "ABC"
    print(min_window(s, t))

blocks.text: This works because the "missing" counter tracks, in O(1), whether every distinct character requirement is currently satisfied, so the window is provably valid exactly when it reaches 0, and greedily shrinking from the left while it stays at 0 is guaranteed to find the smallest valid window reachable from the current right pointer position before validity breaks.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n plus m), since each pointer moves forward across s at most once in total.
Space: O(m), for the character requirement and window count maps.

blocks.text: This is the classic variable size sliding window pattern: expand to satisfy a condition, then greedily shrink as far as possible while the condition still holds, which reappears across many "smallest/largest window satisfying X" problems.

items: Comparing entire count maps for equality on every step instead of tracking a single "missing" counter, which turns each validity check into O(1) instead of O(alphabet size).
Forgetting that t can contain duplicate characters, requiring the window to match counts, not just presence.

blocks.text: Describe the two phases explicitly out loud: an expand phase driven by the right pointer seeking validity, and a contract phase driven by the left pointer seeking the smallest valid window, since naming both phases makes the two pointer logic much easier to reason through.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid recounting every window", think: incremental counts updated as the window expands and shrinks, exactly like Find All Anagrams in a String.
If the interviewer says "how do you check validity quickly", think: a single "missing requirements" counter instead of comparing full count maps.
If the interviewer says "what if t has duplicate characters", think: the count based requirement check already handles this correctly, since it compares exact counts, not just presence.

Any "smallest or largest substring/subarray satisfying a condition" problem, where the expand-then-greedily-shrink two pointer pattern is the standard technique to reach for.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n cubed) time, O(m) space. Optimized: O(n plus m) time, O(m) space.

items: Pattern: a variable size sliding window: expand the right pointer until valid, then greedily shrink the left pointer while it stays valid.

Core Idea: a single "missing requirements" counter tracks overall validity in O(1), letting the window expand to become valid and then shrink to its smallest valid size before expanding again, all in one pass.
Time: O(n cubed) for the brute force, O(n plus m) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(m) for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: once a window is valid, shrinking it as far as possible is always worth attempting, since a smaller valid window can never be a worse answer than a larger one.
Interview Difficulty: the two pointer structure is standard once seen, but correctly maintaining the missing counter through both expansion and contraction is where most bugs occur.
One line memory trick: expand right until valid, shrink left while still valid, repeat.
